Use the same analysis rows

The analysis uses one baseline average per store. X has an intercept and usual delivery days; y is the percentage of stockout product-days averaged over weeks 1–8.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

Least squares minimizes Σ(y−Xβ)². The code solves the linear system using numpy.linalg.lstsq. Fitted values are Xβ and residuals are y−Xβ.

stores = world()['stores']
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(stores)), stores.lead_days])
beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, stores.baseline_rate, rcond=None)[0]
prediction = X @ beta
residual = stores.baseline_rate.to_numpy() - prediction
assert np.isclose(beta[1], lesson_result(4)['slope'])

# Verify the OLS variation decomposition and a log specification.
stores = world()['stores']
x = stores.lead_days.to_numpy()
y = stores.baseline_rate.to_numpy()
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
beta, covariance, residual = fit_ols(X, y)
sst = np.sum((y-y.mean())**2)
sse = np.sum(residual**2)
ssr = np.sum((X@beta-y.mean())**2)
assert np.isclose(sst, sse+ssr)
assert np.isclose(1-sse/sst, lesson_result(4)['depth']['r_squared'])
log_beta, _, log_residual = fit_ols(X, np.log(y))
smearing = np.exp(log_residual).mean()
rate_predictions = np.exp(X@log_beta) * smearing
assert np.isclose(smearing, lesson_result(4)['depth']['forms'][1]['smearing'])

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

The displayed RMSE divides residual squared error by the number of stores before taking the square root. It is a fit measure rather than the residual standard deviation with a degrees-of-freedom correction. Lesson 6 evaluates forecasts on later observations.

Change one analytical choice

Add group means to the fitted line and inspect residuals by delivery time. Ask whether an extra term addresses a visible pattern and whether the resulting comparison remains understandable.

Derive and reproduce the model comparisons

b = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²; a = ȳ − bx̄

Quadratic marginal association = b₁ + 2b₂X; cubic adds 3b₃X²

The variation identity applies to in-sample OLS with an intercept. The local smoother uses a tricube distance weight inside each neighborhood. Log predictions are retransformed using exp(predicted log outcome) multiplied by the mean of exp(training residual). This separates prediction on a log scale from prediction of the arithmetic mean.

stores = world()['stores']
x = stores.lead_days.to_numpy()
y = stores.baseline_rate.to_numpy()
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
beta, covariance, residual = fit_ols(X, y)
sst = ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
sse = (residual ** 2).sum()
r_squared = 1 - sse / sst

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0 = 0.055 + 0.014 × lead + 0.0005 × (demand − 100) + 0.018 × urban + 0.003 × (lead − 3) × urban + 0.020 × promotion + store effect + 0.006 × sin(week / 4)

Expected reduction = 0.006 + 0.008 × lead + 0.004 × urban; p1 = p0 − reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.
